quests.conceptTitle: Comparative Adjectives: Long Adjectives with More
quests.grammarRule: Comparative Adjectives: Long Adjectives with More
quests.correctSentence: This course is more difficult than the last one.
quests.contrastSentence: This course is difficulter than the last one.
quests.ruleExplanation: Longer adjectives (usually two or more syllables) form comparatives with 'more' instead of an ending: more difficult, more expensive. 'Difficulter' isn't a real word.
quests.nativeTip: This adjective has three syllables — too long to just add an ending.

quests.correctSentence: She is happier than her sister; she smiles all day.
quests.contrastSentence: She is more happy than her sister; she smiles all day.
quests.ruleExplanation: Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y still take '-er', changing y to i: happy → happier, easy → easier. They don't need 'more', unlike most other long adjectives.
quests.nativeTip: This two-syllable adjective ends in -y, which changes before the ending.

quests.conceptTitle: Comparative Adjectives: Long Adjectives with More
quests.grammarRule: Comparative Adjectives: Long Adjectives with More
quests.correctSentence: — Which phone is better? — This one is more expensive than that one, but it has more features.
quests.contrastSentence: — Which phone is better? — This one is expensiver than that one, but it has more features.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Expensive' has three syllables, so it needs 'more' rather than an ending: more expensive. This follows the same rule as 'more difficult' from Question 1.
quests.nativeTip: Count the syllables in this adjective — it's too long for an ending.

quests.correctSentence: My cooking is better than it used to be; I've been practicing.
quests.contrastSentence: My cooking is gooder than it used to be; I've been practicing.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Good' has an irregular comparative: better. There's no such word as 'gooder', and 'best' would be the superlative, used for comparing three or more things.
quests.nativeTip: This very common adjective completely changes its form for comparisons.

quests.correctSentence: This year's harvest is worse than last year's, sadly.
quests.contrastSentence: This year's harvest is badder than last year's, sadly.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Bad' has the irregular comparative 'worse'. 'Badder' isn't a real word, and 'worst' is reserved for comparing three or more things.
quests.nativeTip: 'Bad' changes completely, just like 'good' did in the last question.

quests.correctSentence: — How far is the station from here? — It's further than I thought — almost an hour's walk.
quests.contrastSentence: — How far is the station from here? — It's farer than I thought — almost an hour's walk.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Far' has the irregular comparative 'further' (or 'farther'). 'Farer' isn't a word, and 'furthest' would only be used when comparing more than two things.
quests.nativeTip: This adjective also has its own special comparative form.

quests.correctSentence: This is the cheapest restaurant in the whole town.
quests.contrastSentence: This is cheapest restaurant in the whole town.
quests.ruleExplanation: Superlatives usually require 'the' before them: the cheapest. Leaving it out, as in plain 'cheapest', sounds incomplete in a full sentence like this.
quests.nativeTip: Superlatives almost always need one small word in front of them.

quests.correctSentence: He is the tallest student in the entire class.
quests.contrastSentence: He is taller student in the entire class.
quests.ruleExplanation: Comparing one person against an entire group calls for the superlative with 'the': the tallest student. 'Taller' would only compare two people directly.
quests.nativeTip: This compares one person against everyone else in a whole group, not just two people.

quests.correctSentence: — Which day works best for the interview? — Friday is the easiest day for me, out of the whole week.
quests.contrastSentence: — Which day works best for the interview? — Friday is easier day for me, out of the whole week.
quests.ruleExplanation: Comparing against the whole week needs the superlative with 'the': the easiest day. Since 'easy' ends in -y, its superlative changes to '-iest', not 'most easy'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Out of the whole week' signals a comparison against many days, not just two.

quests.conceptTitle: Superlative Adjectives: Long Adjectives with Most
quests.grammarRule: Superlative Adjectives: Long Adjectives with Most
quests.correctSentence: This is the most interesting movie I've ever seen.
quests.contrastSentence: This is more interesting movie I've ever seen.
quests.ruleExplanation: Long adjectives use 'the most' for the superlative: the most interesting. There's no ending like '-est' for long words such as 'interesting'.
quests.nativeTip: This long adjective needs both 'the' and 'most' together.

quests.correctSentence: This is the best meal I've had all week.
quests.contrastSentence: This is the goodest meal I've had all week.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Good' has the irregular superlative 'the best', following the same irregular family as 'better'. 'The goodest' isn't a real form.
quests.nativeTip: Remember the irregular comparative from Level 52 — the superlative changes just as much.

quests.correctSentence: — Which mistake was worst? — Forgetting the tickets was the worst mistake of all.
quests.contrastSentence: — Which mistake was worst? — Forgetting the tickets was the baddest mistake of all.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Bad' has the irregular superlative 'the worst'. 'Worse' would only compare two things, and 'the baddest' isn't standard English.
quests.nativeTip: 'Of all' signals a comparison against every possible mistake, not just two.

quests.correctSentence: My brother is as tall as my father now.
quests.contrastSentence: My brother is as tall than my father now.
quests.ruleExplanation: Equality comparisons follow the pattern 'as + adjective + as': as tall as. 'Than' is only used with comparatives like 'taller than', not with this equal pattern.
quests.nativeTip: Equal comparisons use the same small word on both sides of the adjective.

quests.correctSentence: This test was as difficult as the last one.
quests.contrastSentence: This test was so difficult as the last one.
quests.ruleExplanation: The equality pattern needs 'as' at the start as well as before the second noun: as difficult as. Words like 'so' or 'very' don't complete this specific comparison structure.
quests.nativeTip: The second 'as' later in the sentence tells you what word belongs here too.

quests.correctSentence: — Is your car as fast as mine? — Yes, it's exactly as fast as yours.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is your car as fast as mine? — Yes, it's exactly so fast as yours.
quests.ruleExplanation: The reply mirrors the question's own 'as fast as' structure: it's as fast as yours. This confirms the two things are considered equal.
quests.nativeTip: Match the same structure the question itself already used.

quests.correctSentence: This book isn't as interesting as the movie.
quests.contrastSentence: This book isn't more interesting as the movie.
quests.ruleExplanation: Negative equality still uses 'as...as', just with 'not' added before it: isn't as interesting as. This shows the book is below the movie in interest, without using a comparative form.
quests.nativeTip: Even in the negative, this comparison keeps its usual two matching words.

quests.correctSentence: This book is less interesting than the movie.
quests.contrastSentence: This book is as interesting than the movie.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Than' signals a comparative structure, not an equality one, so 'less' fits here: less interesting than. This expresses the same basic idea as Question 1, but through a different grammatical pattern.
quests.nativeTip: This sentence uses 'than', a word that belongs to a different comparison pattern.

quests.correctSentence: — Is the sequel as good as the original? — Honestly, it's not as good as the first one.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is the sequel as good as the original? — Honestly, it's not so much good as the first one.
quests.ruleExplanation: The reply keeps the same 'as...as' structure as the question, just adding 'not': it's not as good as. This directly answers whether the two things are equal.
quests.nativeTip: The question already used the exact pattern this answer needs to echo.

quests.correctSentence: This coffee is too hot to drink right now.
quests.contrastSentence: This coffee is very hot to drink right now.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Too' shows an excessive amount that causes a negative result: too hot to drink. 'Very' would simply describe intensity without implying you can't actually drink it.
quests.nativeTip: The phrase 'to drink' suggests this quality is causing a problem.

quests.correctSentence: The coffee is very hot, but I can still drink it carefully.
quests.contrastSentence: The coffee is too hot, but I can still drink it carefully.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Very' simply intensifies the adjective without blocking the action, unlike 'too', which would suggest it's impossible to drink. The phrase 'but I can still drink it' confirms this.
quests.nativeTip: Unlike the last question, drinking it is still possible here.

quests.correctSentence: — Can we go hiking today? — No, it's too cold to enjoy it.
quests.contrastSentence: — Can we go hiking today? — No, it's very cold to enjoy it.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Too cold to enjoy it' explains exactly why the answer is 'No' — the cold creates a real obstacle. 'Very cold' alone wouldn't logically explain refusing the plan.
quests.nativeTip: The word 'No' hints that something is preventing this plan.

quests.correctSentence: Is the soup warm enough to serve now?
quests.contrastSentence: Is the soup warm too to serve now?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Enough' comes after an adjective to show sufficiency: warm enough. This is the opposite word order from 'too', which comes before the adjective.
quests.nativeTip: This word describes sufficiency, and it comes right after the adjective.

quests.correctSentence: We don't have enough time to finish this project today.
quests.contrastSentence: We don't have time enough to finish this project today.
quests.ruleExplanation: Before a noun, 'enough' comes first: enough time, enough money. This is different from its position with adjectives, as in 'warm enough' from the last question.
quests.nativeTip: With a noun instead of an adjective, 'enough' switches to the opposite position.

quests.correctSentence: — Do you have enough money for the tickets? — Yes, I think I have just enough .
quests.contrastSentence: — Do you have enough money for the tickets? — Yes, I think I have just too .
quests.ruleExplanation: The reply echoes the question's own word: I have just enough. This means exactly the right amount — not more, not less.
quests.nativeTip: The answer confirms exactly what the question asked about.

quests.correctSentence: — Which hotel is cheaper? — The one downtown is cheaper than this one.
quests.contrastSentence: — Which hotel is cheaper? — The one downtown is cheap than this one.
quests.ruleExplanation: Comparing exactly two things uses the comparative form: cheaper than. The superlative 'cheapest' would only fit if more than two hotels were being compared.
quests.nativeTip: Only two hotels are being compared here.

quests.correctSentence: — Is this the best option? — Yes, it's the best option we have.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is this the best option? — Yes, it's better option we have.
quests.ruleExplanation: Comparing against all available options calls for the superlative with 'the': the best option. This mirrors the question, which already used 'the best'.
quests.nativeTip: This compares against every option available, not just one other choice.

quests.correctSentence: — Is your new job as stressful as the old one? — Actually, it's not as stressful.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is your new job as stressful as the old one? — Actually, it's not so much stressful.
quests.ruleExplanation: The reply reuses the question's 'as...as' pattern with 'not': it's not as stressful. This shows the new job is actually less stressful than the old one.
quests.nativeTip: The question already gave you the exact comparison pattern to reuse.

quests.correctSentence: This suitcase is too small for a two-week trip; I need something bigger.
quests.contrastSentence: This suitcase is enough small for a two-week trip; I need something bigger.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Too small' explains exactly why a bigger suitcase is needed — the current size causes a genuine problem, matching the pattern from Level 57.
quests.nativeTip: The rest of the sentence explains a real problem this size is causing.

quests.correctSentence: Do you have anything less expensive? My budget is limited.
quests.contrastSentence: Do you have anything fewer expensive? My budget is limited.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Less' pairs with adjectives and uncountable ideas like price: less expensive. 'Fewer' would only be correct with countable nouns, like fewer items.
quests.nativeTip: 'Expensive' describes a quality, not something you can count individually.

quests.correctSentence: — Is this the largest size you have? — Yes, it's the largest we carry.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is this the largest size you have? — Yes, it's larger we carry.
quests.ruleExplanation: The answer confirms the superlative with 'the': the largest we carry, comparing this size against every size in stock. This wraps up the comparison, quantity, and sufficiency skills built across Levels 41 to 60.
quests.nativeTip: This closes Stage 3 the same way it opened — with 'the' before a superlative.
